title: Lexical conventions, literals and operator precedence
body: The lexer turns characters into tokens before anything else happens. Integers may contain underscores for readability (`1_000_000`) and be written in hexadecimal (`0xFF`), octal (`0o17`) or binary (`0b1010`). A character literal can be an escape such as `'\n'`, a decimal code `'\065'` or a hexadecimal one `'\x41'`. A string may contain escapes, may continue over a line with a trailing backslash, and may be written in the quoted form `{|...|}` or `{id|...|id}` in which nothing is an escape.

Comments nest: `(* a (* b *) c *)` is one comment, so you can comment out code that already contains comments. Operators are ordinary identifiers made of symbol characters, and their *first* characters decide precedence and associativity: names starting with `+` or `-` are additive and left-associative, `*`, `/` and `%` multiplicative, and `**` right-associative. You may define your own, such as `let ( +++ ) a b = a * 10 + b`.

Function application binds tighter than any operator, so `f x + g y` is `(f x) + (g y)`, and the prefix `-` binds tighter than `*`. `@@` and `|>` are ordinary operators that follow the leading-character rule: `@@` starts with `@`, so it is right-associative and binds more loosely than `+` but more tightly than the comparisons (`f @@ x = y` is `(f @@ x) = y`), while `|>` starts with `|` and sits at the comparison level, grouping from the left. That is why `print_endline @@ string_of_int 3` needs no parentheses. When you are unsure how an expression groups, add parentheses: they cost nothing.

1000000 255 10 15
150.0 2.0
AAA|10
tab:	end
line one continues
raw "quotes" and \n are not escaped
can contain |} inside
123
3
true
512
-6
3
challenge: Define a right-associative operator `**>` such that `1 **> 2 **> 3` means `1 **> (2 **> 3)` using the rule that names starting with `**` are right-associative, with `a **> b = a - b`, and print the result.
solution:
let ( **> ) a b = a - b

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (1 **> 2 **> 3)
question: What decides the precedence and associativity of a user-defined operator?
correct: Its first characters: for example names starting with + or - are additive and left-associative
wrong: The order in which operators are defined
The length of the operator name
reasoning: The language fixes a table by leading characters, so any operator that starts with them inherits that behaviour.

title: Names, namespaces and scope
body: OCaml keeps several namespaces apart, so one spelling can mean different things in different positions: values, type constructors, data constructors, record labels, modules, module types and classes each have their own. `type t = A | B`, `let t = 5`, `module T = struct ... end` and `type r = { t : int }` can all coexist, and the context says which `t` or `T` you mean.

Within one namespace a later definition shadows an earlier one. Constructors are shadowed too: after `type u = A of int`, the name `A` refers to `u` unless a type annotation such as `(A : t)` says otherwise, because OCaml uses the expected type to disambiguate. `type nonrec t = t list` says the right-hand `t` is the *previous* definition, and a qualified name such as `Stdlib.List.length` reaches a module that your own `List` has hidden.

Scope is lexical and nested. `let module M = ... in`, `let open M in` and `M.(expr)` limit a name's reach to one expression. Use shadowing deliberately and sparingly: it is safe for a value you transform step by step, and a trap when it hides a module from the standard library that other code expects.
challenge: Define a module `Option` of your own with a value `get = 0`, then print both `Option.get` and `Stdlib.Option.get (Some 7)` to show how the qualified name reaches the standard one.
solution:
module Option = struct let get = 0 end

let () = Printf.printf "%d %d\n" Option.get (Stdlib.Option.get (Some 7))
question: What does the annotation in `let x : t = A` do when both `t` and `u` have a constructor `A`?
correct: It tells the compiler to pick the constructor of type t instead of the most recent A
wrong: It converts A to a string
It makes the earlier type shadow the later one everywhere
reasoning: OCaml uses the expected type to disambiguate constructors and labels, so the annotation selects the right one.

title: Polymorphism and its limitations
body: Inference is fully automatic for the basic language, but some polymorphism cannot be inferred. A recursive function is monomorphic inside its own body, which breaks *polymorphic recursion*, where the recursive call is at a different type: for `type 'a nested = Flat of 'a | Nested of 'a list nested` the call inside `depth` has type `'a list nested`. You must write the explicit polymorphic annotation `let rec depth : 'a. 'a nested -> int = ...` to tell the checker that the function is polymorphic within its own definition.

A function argument is also monomorphic: `fun f -> (f 1, f "s")` does not type-check because `f` has one type. The way to pass something polymorphic as an argument is *higher-rank polymorphism* through a record with a polymorphic field, `type id = { f : 'a. 'a -> 'a }`, or an object method. Locally abstract types, `fun (type a) (x : a) -> ...`, introduce a type name that the checker treats as abstract inside the body and that you can use in annotations.

These are exactly the places where you add annotations. The compiler error messages point at the recursive call or the argument, and the cure is an explicit `'a.` or a record. If you find yourself needing them often, consider whether a module or functor expresses the same idea more simply.
challenge: Explain in a comment why `depth` needs the explicit `'a.` annotation, then build a value nested three levels deep with `Nested` and print its depth.
solution:
type 'a nested = Flat of 'a | Nested of 'a list nested

(* The recursive call is at type 'a list nested, so depth must be polymorphic
   inside its own body; only the explicit 'a. annotation allows that. *)
let rec depth : 'a. 'a nested -> int = function
  | Flat _ -> 0
  | Nested n -> 1 + depth n

let () = Printf.printf "%d\n" (depth (Nested (Nested (Nested (Flat [ [ [ 1 ] ] ])))))
question: Why does a polymorphically recursive function need an explicit `'a.` annotation?
correct: Inference treats a function as monomorphic inside its own body, so a call at a different type is rejected without the annotation
wrong: Because recursion is not allowed on variants
Because the compiler cannot print polymorphic types
reasoning: The annotation states the function is polymorphic within its own definition, which inference alone cannot discover.

title: Recursive values, recursive modules and mutually recursive types
body: `let rec` is not only for functions. A *value* may be defined in terms of itself if the right-hand side is a constructor application, a record, a lazy value or a function: `let rec ones = 1 :: ones` builds a cyclic list in which the tail points back to the head. The compiler accepts only definitions whose recursion is guarded by such a constructor; something like `let rec evens = 0 :: List.map succ evens` is rejected because the recursive use sits inside a function call.

Types can be mutually recursive with `and`: an expression type that holds statements and a statement type that holds expressions must be defined together. Modules can too, with `module rec A : SIG = ... and B : SIG = ...`; every recursive module needs a full signature so the checker can see through the cycle. Use this sparingly, since it hides the dependency order that normally keeps programs easy to read.

Cyclic data is easy to create and dangerous to traverse: a naive `List.length ones` never terminates, and structural equality or printing of a cycle can loop forever. Always bound the traversal, as `take` does below.
challenge: Define a cyclic list `let rec cycle = 1 :: 2 :: 3 :: cycle` and print its first seven elements with a bounded `take`.
question: Why must every recursive module have a full signature?
correct: The checker needs to see the interface of each module to type the references across the cycle
wrong: So the modules can be compiled in any order at runtime
Because recursive modules cannot contain functions
reasoning: Without declared signatures the modules would depend on each other's inferred types, which does not terminate, so the interfaces break the cycle.

title: Private types, extensible variants and inline records
body: A *private* type abbreviation, `type t = private float`, can be read as a float (`(m :> float)`) but cannot be created except through the module's own functions. It is a lightweight abstract type: users keep the convenience of the representation while you keep control over how values are made, which is useful for validated numbers such as lengths that must not be negative.

An *extensible variant* type, declared `type event = ..`, has no fixed list of cases; any module can add constructors with `type event += Click of int`. Exceptions are the best-known example: `exn` is an extensible type. A match must end with a catch-all `_` case because new constructors may appear later, which makes extensible types the right tool for plug-in style events and the wrong one when you want exhaustiveness checking.

*Inline records* give a constructor named fields, `Circle of { radius : float }`, without a separate record type. The record is not a first-class value and cannot escape the pattern that binds it, which avoids an allocation and keeps the fields close to the constructor that owns them. Choose them when a constructor has several fields that are easy to confuse positionally.
code:
module Meters : sig
  type t = private float

  val of_float : float -> t
  val to_float : t -> float
end = struct
  type t = float

  let of_float x = if x < 0. then invalid_arg "negative length" else x
  let to_float x = x
end

type event = ..
type event += Click of int | Key of char

let describe = function
  | Click n -> Printf.sprintf "click %d" n
  | Key c -> Printf.sprintf "key %c" c
  | _ -> "unknown event"

type event += Scroll

type shape = Circle of { radius : float } | Rect of { w : float; h : float }

let area = function
  | Circle { radius } -> 3. *. radius *. radius
  | Rect { w; h } -> w *. h

let () =
  let m = Meters.of_float 2.5 in
  Printf.printf "%.1f %.1f\n" (m :> float) (Meters.to_float m);
  (try ignore (Meters.of_float (-1.)) with Invalid_argument msg -> print_endline msg);
  List.iter (fun e -> print_endline (describe e)) [ Click 3; Key 'x'; Scroll ];
  Printf.printf "%.1f %.1f\n" (area (Circle { radius = 2. })) (area (Rect { w = 2.; h = 4.5 }))
expectedStdout:
2.5 2.5
negative length
click 3
key x
unknown event
12.0 9.0
challenge: Add a `Triangle of { base : float; height : float }` inline-record constructor with area half the base times the height, and print its area for base 4 and height 3.
question: Why must a match on an extensible variant end with a catch-all case?
correct: Other modules can add constructors later, so the compiler can never know every case
wrong: Because extensible variants have only one constructor
Because the match would be too slow
reasoning: The set of constructors is open, so exhaustiveness cannot be checked and a wildcard handles whatever is added.

title: Attributes and extension points
body: An *attribute*, written `[@name payload]` on an expression or `[@@name]` on a declaration, attaches information to the syntax tree. The compiler understands a few: `[@inline]` asks for a function to be inlined, `[@tailcall]` makes the compiler warn if a call is not a tail call, `[@deprecated "message"]` makes uses of a definition produce an alert, `[@@unboxed]` removes the box around a single-constructor type, and `[@warning "-8"]` changes warnings for a region.

Unknown attributes are ignored by the compiler and left for PPX rewriters to read, which is how `[@@deriving show]` works. An *extension point*, `[%name payload]`, is different: it marks a place where a rewriter must produce code, and the compiler rejects an extension node that no rewriter has handled. Attributes annotate code; extension points ask for code.

Because `[@@unboxed]` changes the runtime representation, `Id 5` is stored as the integer 5 itself. You can observe that with `Obj.is_int`, a function meant for debugging and not for production code. Use attributes for performance tuning only after measuring, since the compiler already inlines small functions without being asked.
challenge: Mark a recursive `count_down` function with `[@tailcall]` on its recursive call and a `[@inline]` helper, and print `count_down 100000`.
question: What is the difference between `[@name]` and `[%name]`?
correct: An attribute annotates existing code, while an extension point marks a place a rewriter must replace with code
wrong: They are two spellings of the same thing
Attributes run at runtime and extension points at compile time
reasoning: Attributes are metadata the compiler may ignore; extension nodes must be expanded by a rewriter or compilation fails.

title: The module system in depth: substitution, aliases and functor styles
body: A signature constraint `S with type t = int` makes the abstract type equal to `int`, and keeps `t` in the signature. *Destructive substitution*, `S with type t := int`, goes further and removes `t` from the signature, replacing every use by `int`. It is the neat way to specialise a generic signature without leaving a redundant type behind.

A *module alias*, `module M = List`, makes `M` another name for the same module, with no copy and no new types. A functor can be *applicative* (`module F (X : S) = ...`), where applying it twice to the same argument yields compatible types, or *generative* (`module G () = ...`), where each application creates fresh abstract types. Generativity is what you want when each application should own distinct state or types, such as a unique-identifier generator.

`module type of M` gives the signature of an existing module, and `include` copies a module's contents into another, so a wrapper module can extend a library module by including it and adding functions. These tools together let you reshape module interfaces after the fact, which is how large libraries expose a small public API over a big implementation.
code:
module type S = sig
  type t

  val x : t
  val show : t -> string
end

module type S_int = S with type t := int

module A : S_int = struct
  let x = 5
  let show = string_of_int
end

module L = List

module Fresh () : sig
  type id

  val next : unit -> id
  val to_int : id -> int
end = struct
  type id = int

  let counter = ref 0
  let next () = incr counter; !counter
  let to_int i = i
end

module Ids1 = Fresh ()
module Ids2 = Fresh ()

module Extended_list = struct
  include List

  let second = function _ :: x :: _ -> Some x | _ -> None
end

let () =
  Printf.printf "%s %d\n" (A.show A.x) (A.x + 1);
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (L.length [ 1; 2; 3 ]);
  let a = Ids1.next () in
  let b = Ids1.next () in
  let c = Ids2.next () in
  Printf.printf "%d %d %d\n" (Ids1.to_int a) (Ids1.to_int b) (Ids2.to_int c);
  Printf.printf "%s\n" (match Extended_list.second [ 10; 20; 30 ] with Some n -> string_of_int n | None -> "none")
challenge: Create a second generative instance `Ids3 = Fresh ()` and show that its counter starts again at 1 by printing the first id it returns.
solution:
module Fresh () : sig
  type id

  val next : unit -> id
  val to_int : id -> int
end = struct
  type id = int

  let counter = ref 0
  let next () = incr counter; !counter
  let to_int i = i
end

module Ids1 = Fresh ()
module Ids3 = Fresh ()

let () =
  ignore (Ids1.next ());
  ignore (Ids1.next ());
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (Ids3.to_int (Ids3.next ()))
question: What is the difference between `S with type t = int` and `S with type t := int`?
correct: With = keeps t in the signature as an equation; with := removes t and replaces its uses by int
wrong: They are identical
The first applies to values and the second to types
reasoning: Destructive substitution deletes the abstract type from the signature, leaving a smaller interface.

title: Classes, inheritance and virtual methods
body: A class describes objects with state (`val`) and behaviour (`method`). `inherit parent` reuses the parent's fields and methods, `object (self) ... end` gives the object a name for calling its own methods with `self#m`, and `inherit parent as super` lets an override call `super#m`. A *virtual* class declares methods without implementing them (`method virtual area : float`) and cannot be instantiated, so it works as an abstract base whose subclasses must fill the gaps.

An `initializer` block runs when an object is created, after the fields are set. Objects are mutable by default through `val mutable`, but an *immutable* style works too: the functional update `{< x = x + d >}` returns a copy of the object with some fields changed. Classes can be polymorphic, `class ['a] stack`, and a *class type* lists the methods an object must have without any implementation.

Method calls are resolved at runtime through the object, which is *open recursion*: a method in a parent calling `self#area` uses the subclass's `area`. That flexibility is what objects offer beyond modules and records, and its price is weaker static guarantees and harder reasoning. Most OCaml code reaches for modules first and keeps classes for open-ended extension.
code:
class virtual shape name =
  object (self)
    method virtual area : float
    method describe = Printf.sprintf "%s with area %.1f" name self#area
  end

class circle r = object inherit shape "circle" method area = 3.0 *. r *. r end
class square s = object inherit shape "square" method area = s *. s end

class big_circle r =
  object
    inherit circle r as super
    method! area = super#area *. 2.0
  end

class greeter name =
  object
    initializer print_endline ("created " ^ name)
    method hi = "hi " ^ name
  end

class point x =
  object
    val x = x
    method get = x
    method move d = {< x = x + d >}
  end

class ['a] stack =
  object
    val items : 'a list = []
    method push (v : 'a) = {< items = v :: items >}
    method top = match items with [] -> None | v :: _ -> Some v
  end

class type printable = object method describe : string end

let () =
  let shapes : printable list = [ (new circle 1.0 :> printable); (new square 2.0 :> printable); (new big_circle 1.0 :> printable) ] in
  List.iter (fun s -> print_endline s#describe) shapes;
  let g = new greeter "ada" in
  print_endline g#hi;
  let p = new point 1 in
  let q = p#move 5 in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" p#get q#get;
  let s = (new stack)#push 1 in
  let s = s#push 2 in
  Printf.printf "%s\n" (match s#top with Some n -> string_of_int n | None -> "empty")
expectedStdout:
circle with area 3.0
square with area 4.0
circle with area 6.0
created ada
hi ada
1 6
2
challenge: Add a `triangle base height` class that inherits `shape` and implements `area`, and print the description of `new triangle 4.0 3.0`.
solution:
class virtual shape name =
  object (self)
    method virtual area : float
    method describe = Printf.sprintf "%s with area %.1f" name self#area
  end

class triangle base height =
  object
    inherit shape "triangle"
    method area = base *. height /. 2.0
  end

let () = print_endline (new triangle 4.0 3.0)#describe
question: What makes a class `virtual`?
correct: It declares at least one method without implementing it, so it cannot be instantiated directly
wrong: It runs its methods on another thread
Its fields are always immutable
reasoning: A virtual class is an abstract base: subclasses must supply the missing methods before objects can be created.

title: A tour of the standard library
body: The standard library is a set of modules named for the types they serve, all opened by default through `Stdlib`: `Int`, `Float`, `Char`, `Bool`, `String`, `Bytes`, `Option`, `Result`, `Either`, `Fun`, `Lazy`, `Seq`, `List`, `Array`, `Stack`, `Queue`, `Hashtbl`, `Map`, `Set`, `Buffer`, `Format`, `Scanf`, `Filename`, `Digest`, `In_channel` and `Out_channel`. Learning the library is largely learning which module holds the function you need, so the module name is the first place to look.

The conventions repeat across modules: a type `t`, `create`/`of_...` constructors, `to_string`, `compare`, `equal`, and `_opt` variants that return an option instead of raising. A module with `compare` and `t` can be passed to `Map.Make` or `Set.Make`, which is why `Int`, `String` and `Float` all provide them. Functions that may fail come in pairs, such as `List.find` and `List.find_opt`.

The tour below touches many modules with deterministic output. Reading the documentation for a module you rarely use is cheap compared with rewriting what it already does, and the OCaml manual lists every module with its types and functions.

2 true true
9 left 3
2 1
3
24 ABC
file.txt .gz
6217c07ff169f6ab2eb2731f855095f1
hello+world

challenge: Use `Scanf.sscanf` to parse the string "7,4" with the format "%d,%d" and print the sum, then print `Filename.remove_extension "report.pdf"`.
question: Why do many standard modules provide both `find` and `find_opt` style functions?
correct: One raises an exception when nothing matches and the other returns an option, so callers can choose how to handle absence
wrong: They search in different directions
One is for lists and the other for arrays
reasoning: The _opt variants make absence part of the return type, which is usually safer than catching an exception.

title: How values are laid out in memory
body: Every OCaml value is one machine word. An *immediate* value, such as an `int`, a `char`, a `bool`, `()`, `[]`, `None` or a constant constructor, is stored directly with its lowest bit set, so it needs no allocation. Anything else is a pointer to a *block* in the heap, which begins with a header recording the block's size in words and a *tag* byte, followed by the fields.

The tag tells the runtime and the garbage collector what the block holds. Constructors with arguments are numbered in order of declaration starting at 0, separately from the constant constructors, so `type c = A | B of int | C of int * int` stores `A` as an immediate, `B 1` as a one-field block with tag 0, and `C (1, 2)` as a two-field block with tag 1. Tuples, records, `Some x` and list cells are blocks with tag 0, floats and strings have special tags, and a float array is stored unboxed.

The `Obj` module can look at this layout, which is the way to see it for yourself, but it bypasses the type system and its functions can crash a program if misused. Use it for exploration and never for application logic. Knowing the layout explains costs such as why a list of floats allocates a box per element while a `float array` does not.

immediate 0

question: How is the constant constructor `A` of `type c = A | B of int` stored?
correct: As an immediate integer, with no heap block
wrong: As a block with tag 0 and size 0
As a pointer to a shared static string
reasoning: Constant constructors carry no data, so the runtime represents them as small tagged integers in the word itself.
